name: Freya Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice with a small line contractor in our market town, Baker and Hale, which my uncle co-owns. There are fourteen of us, and we do work for the power company: new connections for farms and housing, pole changes, the odd storm job when their own crews are stretched. I'm on a crew most days, learning to frame poles and set transformers, and I'm still slower than I'd like. But I'm the one who sorted out how the firm uses AI, so I get pulled into the office more than most apprentices.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that office work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I set up an AI tool that reads the power company's job specs and drafts our quotes, and my uncle checks them. It's cut his quoting time in half, and I use the same tools every day for my own study and my logbook. Callum, my partner, is a farm mechanic, and we've got about nine months saved, plus I bought a little garage unit in town that I rent out. I believe in working for what you've got, and I want to own a firm like this one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still worth using, even if the hype was overdone. At the firm I'd say we got a cheaper quoting system out of it and that's that. Online I'd probably post something about small firms getting a fair shot without big tech eating everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. The firm keeps its power company contracts, I finish the apprenticeship in three years, and I keep helping my uncle with the business side. It might even be easier, with no big firms racing ahead with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for quotes and logbooks, and keep pushing to finish my ticket. I'd look at buying a second garage unit, because the first one pays well. And I'd ask my uncle to let me sit in on contract meetings, so I learn the business side properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a steady world, and steady suits a small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you want to own a firm, rather than work for the power company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like building something. The power company's crews are good, but you're a number there. At a small firm, if you work hard and think ahead, you can end up owning a piece of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in this world that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing a contract. The power company tenders every three years, and if a bigger contractor undercuts us, we'd struggle. That's always been the risk for firms our size, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity for firms that move first. I'd tell my uncle and the other owners that we need to be ahead of this, not behind. Online I'd share what we're doing, because small firms can learn from each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for us. AI does the quoting, the planning, the scheduling, and we stay lean. The crews still do the climbing for years, so the work's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the firm to put AI into scheduling and route planning this year, and offer to set it up. I'd keep studying for my ticket. And I'd start a small side thing helping other small contractors set up AI quoting, maybe for a few hundred a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the older owners think of you pushing this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hale, my uncle's partner, would grumble. He's old-school. But he'd come round once he sees the numbers, he always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the firm who'd lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our part-time bookkeeper, probably. I'd suggest we keep her on for the checking, at least at first. The AI makes mistakes, so someone at the firm has to catch them, and that's a job worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small firms need to adapt fast or get swallowed. I wouldn't ask for handouts, but I'd want rules that don't let the biggest firms lock everyone else out of robots. I'd raise that with our local representative and the contractors' association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a real threat to us. AGI by 2028 means the power company can plan and quote everything itself, and by 2031 the big contractors would have robot crews. A fourteen-person firm like ours can't buy a robot fleet. I'd have three years to find our place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push my uncle to look at leasing robots early, or partnering with a bigger firm. I'd move some savings into the business if it needs it. And I'd keep the garage unit as our safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not scared for myself, I'd find work, but I'd be worried about the firm and everyone in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth: that we're working on it, and that the firm might change shape. Some of the older guys would retire early, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to own a firm in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but a different kind. Maybe one that runs and maintains robots for the power company, instead of crews. That's where I'd aim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for small firms to get ready, if they start now. I'd tell other owners at the contractors' association to stop waiting for the power company to tell them what to do. Online I'd share what we're trying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's manageable. By 2031 I'd have my ticket and a bigger role in the firm, and the quoting and planning would already be AI work. Robots at 2034 give us three more years to lease or partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the firm to trial a robot in 2032, before everyone else, even if it's a small one for pole inspections. I'd keep the side business going and buy the second garage unit. And I'd keep some savings back in case the firm needs a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy way. There's lots to do and not much time to sit and worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you feel calm about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot actually work on our lines, and knowing we could afford it, would make me calm. Until then, I'd be planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be close to retiring by 2034. I think he'd hand more to me, which is what I want anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and firms that don't prepare only have themselves to blame. I'd encourage apprentices to learn the tools early, the way I did. At the contractors' association I'd push for shared training on robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is a good one for me. By 2036 I could own part of the firm, and the office side would be fully AI by then. By 2039 I'd be ready to bring in robots on my terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my ticket, buy into the firm over a few years, and keep investing in garage units. I'd plan the robot move for the late 2030s, step by step. Callum and I would probably buy a house first, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It fits my plans almost exactly, which is a strange thing to say about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids about work, in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade and learn the tools. Own something if you can. That's what's worked for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd lose in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the crew feeling. When robots come, the yard gets quieter, and I'd miss the crew feeling. That's the part money doesn't replace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the big firms would get robots first and squeeze small ones like ours. What would help is fair rules so small firms can lease robots too, and my uncle letting me take on more of the business side now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about small firms. Everyone talks about workers and big companies, but family firms are where a lot of us learn the trade.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about workers and big companies, but family firms are where a lot of us learn the trade.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old apprentice** at a small family line contractor her uncle co-owns.
She uses **AI every day** and set up the firm's AI quoting system.
She has **nine months saved** and a rented garage unit, and wants to own a firm.
She's calm in slow pictures but **anxious** for the firm when robots arrive by 2031.
Her plan is to **reshape the firm** around robots rather than compete with big rivals.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **big firms** would get robots first and squeeze small ones.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair rules** so small firms can lease robots, and more business responsibility now.
